name: Qubits Are Extremely Fragile
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Handle With Care: Why Qubits Break So Easily
lesson.summary: Describes the practical fragility of qubits compared to classical bits, including short coherence times and the extreme physical isolation required to protect quantum information.
lesson.body:
Decoherence, covered in the previous section, sets a time budget on how long a qubit's quantum information stays usable. Qubits are, in practical terms, extremely fragile compared to classical bits, and this section makes that fragility concrete. Depending on the physical platform and the specific technology generation, coherence times for real qubits today are typically measured in ranges from microseconds up to a few milliseconds, figures that continue to improve with better materials and engineering but remain, by the standards of classical electronics, remarkably short lived.

The contrast with classical memory is stark. A classical bit stored in flash memory can reliably hold its value for years with no active intervention at all, and even a bit held in the faster but more volatile DRAM used in a computer's working memory is refreshed thousands of times per second and, for practical purposes, never spontaneously loses its value in a way a user would notice. A qubit's usable lifetime, by comparison, is closer to a candle in the wind: any computation involving it has to complete within a window that is fleeting on human timescales, even though it can still be long enough, in absolute terms, for thousands of fast quantum gate operations, since individual gates on some platforms take only nanoseconds.

This time pressure shapes how quantum algorithms have to be designed and run in practice. Every gate operation is itself imperfect, and every additional gate consumes some of the finite coherence budget while also adding its own small chance of error, a topic taken up directly in the next section. The practical result is that a real quantum circuit can only include so many operations before the accumulated effects of decoherence and imperfect gates overwhelm whatever useful signal the algorithm was trying to produce, which is why the number of gates a given generation of hardware can reliably run, sometimes called its circuit depth, is one of the most closely watched figures in the field, arguably more important than the raw number of qubits alone.

Engineers respond to this fragility with extreme physical isolation, since protecting coherence is fundamentally about minimizing unwanted interaction with the environment. Superconducting qubit chips sit at the bottom of dilution refrigerators, cooled to roughly a few hundredths of a degree above absolute zero, colder than anywhere in deep space, inside multiple nested shields against stray magnetic fields and vibration. Trapped ion systems require ultra high vacuum chambers and precisely stabilized lasers. None of this apparatus fits on a desk, and much of the cost and complexity of building a quantum computer today goes into this isolation rather than into the qubits themselves.

This is also why scaling a quantum computer is not simply a matter of adding more qubits the way adding more transistors scales a classical chip. Each additional qubit is another fragile quantum system that must be controlled and read out without introducing new noise into its neighbors, and the wiring, cooling, and control electronics needed to manage many qubits at once become their own significant engineering challenge. Fragility, more than any single number like error rate or qubit count, is the underlying reason quantum computing has taken decades to progress from proof of concept to today's still limited machines.
